abstract.p: Low-dose interleukin 2 (Ld-IL2) has shown therapeutic effects in autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), yet optimal dosage has not been established in clinical trials. In this multicentre, double-blind, phase IIb trial, 152 patients with active SLE were randomised (1:1:1:1) to receive subcutaneous IL2 (0.2, 0.5, or 1.0 million IU) or placebo every other day for 12 weeks, then weekly for another 12 weeks. At week 12, SRI-4 response rates were higher in the IL2 1 M IU (69.7%), 0.5 M IU (64.7%), and 0.2 M IU (42.9%) groups than the placebo control group (23.5%). Notably, these differences persisted until week 24 (P < 0.001). Moreover, achievement of LLDAS increased in a dose-dependent manner. Patients who received 1 M IU also showed significant reductions in PGA scores, anti-dsDNA antibody titres and prednisone dosages. Infection rates were lower in the IL2 groups compared with placebo. Ld-IL2 drove the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and altered Treg/effector T cell ratios. These findings highlight the dose-dependent efficacy of IL2 with a favourable safety profile. (Clinicaltrials.gov registration number: NCT04077684).

Low-dose IL-2 therapy has been evaluated for the treatment of numerous autoimmune conditions. This study reports the outcomes of a phase 2, randomised, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of low-dose IL-2 for the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease characterised by chronic immune dysregulation that affects multiple organs, leading to inflammation and tissue damage, and elevates patient mortality1. While conventional treatments, such as immunosuppressants and glucocorticoids, can partially manage disease activity, they often come with significant side effects, including a higher risk of infections. Infections are a leading cause of hospitalisations and mortality among SLE patients. Therefore, there is a need for innovative therapies that can selectively modulate immune responses, improving patient outcomes while minimising the risk of infections.

Interleukin-2 (IL2) is a cytokine that plays a critical role in regulating the immune system. It is well-known for its ability to promote the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs), which are essential for maintaining immune tolerance2. Recent studies on low-dose IL2 (Ld-IL2) therapy have shown promising results in selectively expanding Treg cells without excessively activating effector T cells3–5. This distinctive mechanism allows Ld-IL2 to reduce disease activity in SLE while preserving the necessary functions of the immune system to prevent infections.

In recent years, Ld-IL2 has shown therapeutic efficacy across a broad spectrum of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Sjögren’s syndrome (SS), and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM)6–9. In addition, Ld-IL2 has been investigated for its immunomodulatory effects in conditions like type 1 diabetes (T1D), infection, acute myocardial infarction (AMI), neurodegenerative disorders and most recently amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)10–13. Ld-IL2 at largely different doses ranging from 0.33 to 3 million units, is effective in reducing disease activity in patients with autoimmune diseases, though conducted in different cohorts with limited sample size14–16. However, the optimal dosage for SLE is not clear, leading to difficulty in dosing decisions and uncertain efficacy in clinical practice. It is also important to define the therapeutic window that expands Tregs without stimulating effector T cells.

Thus, this multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIb study was designed to evaluate the relationship between IL2 dose and efficacy, safety and immune responses in patients with active SLE. It focuses on disease activity, serological parameters, safety profiles, and Tregs expansion and maintenance in a period of 24 weeks.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and baseline comparison across treatment groups
sec.p:
Of the 160 patients who underwent screening for eligibility, 152 met the criteria for inclusion in the trial and were randomly allocated to receive IL2 0.2 M IU (n = 38), IL2 0.5 M IU (n = 38), IL2 1.0 M IU (n = 37) or placebo (n = 39); 136 (89.5%) patients completed the 24-week double-blind period (Fig. 1). The demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients at baseline were comparable among the treatment groups. Baseline immunosuppressive therapy and the effects of body surface area (BSA) on dosage were similar in each group, with no statistical significance (Table 1). The median age of the patients was 37.5 ± 12.2 years old, and 131/136 patients (96.3%) were female. All the patients with a median duration of 5 years (IQR 1.1–10.0). At baseline, 124 (91.2%) participants were receiving glucocorticoids with a mean prednisone dose (or equivalent) of 16.2 ± 13.0 mg per day (median dose of 10.0 [IQR7.5–22.0]).Fig. 1Trial profile.

sec.title: Expansion of regulatory T cells and restoration of immune balance in a dose-dependent manner
sec.p:
Flow cytometry analysis revealed that IL2 led to an increase in CD4+ T cell counts across all IL2 groups, with the most significant expansion occurring in the 1 M IU group (P = 0.045, Fig. S1A). Furthermore, all IL2 treatments promoted the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs), as significant increases in CD3+CD4+CD25highfoxp3+ Tregs in the 1 M IU group at week 12 (all P < 0.05; Fig. 2A, B). Following the change in dosing frequency from every other day to once per week, a general decline in foxp3+Tregs and CD3+CD4+CD25highCD127low Tregs was also observed across all IL2 treated groups (Figs. 2A, B and S1B). It is noted that CD3⁺CD4⁺CD25⁻Foxp3⁻ T conventional cells (Tconv) significantly declined after 1 M IU treatment in 12 weeks, and the balance of regulatory and effector T cells was maintained during the follow-up period (all P < 0.05; Fig. 2C, D).Fig. 2Dynamics of laboratory and immunological responses after IL2 treatment.

Data are shown as mean ± SEM and differences between the four groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U test. Red represents Ld-IL2 1 M IU versus placebo group; blue Ld-IL2 0.5 M IU versus placebo group; yellow represents Ld-IL2 0.2 M IU versus placebo group. Ld-IL2, low-dose interleukin 2. sec.title: Ld-IL2 demonstrates a dose-efficacy relationship in SLE
sec.p:
At week 12, treatment with Ld-IL2 demonstrated significant improvements in the SLE Responder Index 4 (SRI-4) response rates in the 1 M IU group (23/33, 69.7%, P < 0.001), 0.5 M IU group (22/34, 64.7%, P < 0.001) than the placebo (15/35, 23.5%). The 0.2 M IU group also showed a higher percentage (42.9%) compared to placebo, although not statistically significant (P = 0.089) (Fig. 3A and Table 2). The significant difference proceeded until the end of the treatment period at week 24 (P < 0.001; Fig. 3B). Additionally, a clear dose-dependent trend was observed at week 12 and 24, suggesting greater clinical efficacy with increasing doses of Ld-IL2 (Table 2). Both the 1 M IU and 0.5 M IU groups achieved significant and sustained improvements in SLEDAI scores compared with placebo throughout the treatment period (all P < 0.05; Fig. 3C and Table 2).Fig. 3The clinical efficacy through 24 weeks in overall study population.

At week 12, the proportions of participants achieving Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS) responses were significantly higher in the Ld-IL2 1 M IU group (9/33, 27.3%; P = 0.006), the 0.5 M IU group (7/34, 20.6%; P = 0.027) compared to the placebo group (1/34, 2.9%). The response rate in the 0.2 M IU group appeared higher (5/35, 14.3%) than that of placebo, but this was not statistically significant (P = 0.094). These response rates further increased to 51.5%, 37.1%, and 28.5% respectively in 1 M IU, 0.5 M IU and 0.2 M IU at week 24 (Fig. 3D). Additionally, patients receiving 1 M IU and 0.5 M IU Ld-IL2, rather than 0.2 M IU demonstrated a significant reduction in PGA scores compared with those in the placebo group (all P < 0.05, Fig. 3E). Furthermore, the 1 MIU Ld-IL2 group exhibited a more significant decline in Physician’s Global Assessment (PGA) scores compared to the other 2 doses, 0.5 MIU (P = 0.035) and 0.2 MIU (P = 0.015) group at week 24 (Table 2).

sec.title: Improvements in organ involvement and steroid tapering
sec.p: At week 12, the 1 MIU Ld-IL2 group had significantly more patients achieving improvement in the mucocutaneous (P = 0.004) and haematological domains (P = 0.013) than the placebo group (Table 2). Furthermore, the Ld-IL2 1 M IU demonstrated significantly higher percentage reductions in the mucocutaneous domain compared to both the placebo (P = 0.004) and 0.2 MIU groups (P = 0.017) by week 24, with numerically superior outcomes relative to the 0.5 M IU dose group (Table 2). Significant reduction in urine protein was observed at week 12 in 1 M IU Ld-IL2 compared with the placebo group (P = 0.036) and Ld-IL2 0.2 MIU (P = 0.027), with numerically superior outcomes relative to the 0.5 M IU dose group (P = 0.414) (Table 2). The decrease in 1 M IU group was sustained throughout the treatment period by week 24 (P = 0.050, Table 2).

Prednisone dosage during the treatment period was reduced in all Ld-IL2 therapies compared with the placebo group. Notably, the 1 M IU Ld-IL2 achieved sustained corticosteroid tapering and demonstrated a significant reduction at week 24 compared to placebo (P = 0.001) (Fig. 3F, Table 2).

Serological parameters indicated increased C3 and C4 levels starting from week 4 in all IL-2 groups (Fig. 4A, B). Statistically significant increases in C3 were observed at week 12 for both the 0.5 M IU (P = 0.021) and 1 M IU (P = 0.017) groups compared to placebo (Fig. 4A and Table 2). However, following the transition of administration schedule to once a week, the complement components revealed a tendency to decrease, and only Ld-IL2 in 1 M IU presented a stable maintenance. In addition, a significant decrease in anti-dsDNA antibody titres was observed with 1 M IU Ld-IL2 treatment at week 12 (P = 0.012) compared to the placebo and maintained through week 24 (P = 0.040) (Table 2).Fig. 4Dynamics of laboratory and immunological responses after IL2 treatment.

A modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analysis was also performed, including all randomised patients who received at least one dose of study treatment, and the results were comparable to those obtained by per-protocol (PP) analysis (Supplementary Table 1).

sec.title: Favourable safety profile and lower infection rates following Ld-IL2 treatment
sec.p:
Treatment with IL-2 was generally well tolerated, and treatment-related adverse events were mostly transient and mild to moderate in severity (Table 3). The most often reported adverse events were injection site reactions with 2 (5.3%), 6 (15.8%), 10 (27%), and 0 (0%) in the IL-2 0.2 M IU, 0.5 M IU, 1 M IU, and placebo group. Among 152 patients, there were fewer infections in all the Ld-IL2 group compared with the placebo group. One case of upper respiratory tract infection and no urinary tract infection were respectively reported in all the Ld-IL2 group, whereas 3 patients (7.7%) had upper respiratory tract infections, and 2 (5.1%) had urinary tract infections in the placebo group during the trial. Among patients enroled after December 2022, several developed mild respiratory symptoms consistent with Omicron infection. However, the majority of these cases were not recorded as adverse events, given their limited clinical significance and resolution without intervention.Table 3

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase IIb, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of Ld-IL2 across three dosing levels (0.2 M IU, 0.5 M IU, and 1 M IU) in patients with active SLE. These doses were selected based on insights from previous studies, with particular consideration given to the safety profile of Ld-IL215–19. Therefore, multiple studies identified increased side effects with more concern at doses >1.5M IU16,20,21. The stepwise escalation aimed to identify the maximum effective and tolerated doses within a unified trial design. The dosing frequency (every other day for twelve weeks followed by weekly administration) was selected to balance sustained Treg expansion with patient tolerability and convenience. Previous studies have indicated that higher doses of Ld-IL2 are associated with increased incidence and severity of varied adverse effects, such as systemic reactions, including fever, chills, and flu-like symptom14,17,22. To balance efficacy and safety in SLE, 1.5 M IU daily for five days followed by biweekly injections was used, achieving clinical and immunological improvements but with notable injection-related adverse events and limited long-term data15,16. Similarly, other studies applied short-course IL2 pulses (1–3 MIU/day) in type 1 diabetes and HCV-induced vasculitis, reporting transient Treg expansion and symptom relief alongside systemic reactions23,24. Consequently, the dosages used in this study struck an optimal balance between achieving effective clinical outcomes and maintaining acceptable safety and tolerability for patients with SLE.

Our findings demonstrate dose-dependent efficacy, with the 1 M IU and 0.5 M IU groups showing significantly higher efficacy than the placebo group. In particular, the 1 M IU dose, achieved the primary endpoint of a significant SRI-4 response in a greater proportion of patients, with notable improvements in mucocutaneous and haematological domains by week 12.

Additionally, over 50% of patients in 1 M IU groups achieved LLDAS at week 24, an important indicator of effective disease control, underscoring the potential of Ld-IL2 to manage SLE comprehensively. The steroid-sparing effect noted in this study highlights the clinical effectiveness of Ld-IL2, especially in the 1 M IU group, which is particularly beneficial given the long-term side effects that can arise from steroid use.

Notably, the 1 M IU dose demonstrated a favourable safety profile, with no significant increase in AEs. In contrast, higher doses of IL2 above 1 M IU were associated with more severe side effects, leading to increased discontinuation rates among patients21, suggesting a dose-dependent relationship. Previous studies reported increased AEs and higher dropout rates at the 3 M IU dose14. This finding underscores the critical challenge of balancing therapeutic efficacy with safety when using higher doses of Ld-IL2.

Safety was an important clinical consideration, and Ld-IL2 showed a favourable safety profile across all dosage groups. AEs were generally mild to moderate, with injection site reactions being the most commonly reported side effect, especially in the 1.0 M IU dose group. Importantly, Ld-IL2 treatment was associated with a lower infection rate than placebo. Only one upper respiratory infection was reported in the Ld-IL2 groups, compared to five cases (including respiratory and urinary tract infections) in the placebo group. This low infection rate is clinically significant, contrasting with traditional immunosuppressive therapies that often elevate infection risks. These findings suggest that Ld-IL2 may provide a safer therapeutic option by promoting immune tolerance without broad immunosuppression.

The clinical benefits observed in this trial are likely attributable to the preferential expansion of Tregs over Tconv by IL225. The 1 million IU dose significantly increased the Foxp3+Tregs and restored the balance between Tregs and effector T cells. This restoration contributed to the observed immunoregulatory and anti-inflammatory effects. Moreover, the significant reduction in circulating anti-dsDNA antibody levels in the 1 million IU group, compared to the placebo group, suggests a mechanistic link between Treg expansion and decreased autoimmune activity in SLE.

Despite these promising findings, this study has several limitations. The relatively small sample size in the 0.2 M IU group has limited the statistical power to detect significant differences in clinical subtypes and biomarkers (e.g. autoantibodies and proteinuria). Nevertheless, a clear dose-dependent trend was consistently observed across the study outcomes. Although the 24-week trial duration was adequate for assessing primary outcomes, it may not fully capture the long-term safety and efficacy, especially regarding sustained Treg expansion. Additionally, the study did not assess variability in patient responses based on clinical or immunologic factors, which could influence individual outcomes with low-dose IL2 therapy. Future studies with larger, more diverse cohorts and longer follow-up periods are needed to validate these findings and improve dosing strategies. Furthermore, the detailed Treg kinetics were not studied in this trial since IL2-Treg kinetics association has been shown in several previous studies16,20.

The findings of this study will enhance our understanding of IL-2’s immunomodulatory mechanisms in SLE and offer practical insights for optimising IL2 dosing in the management of autoimmune diseases. This will facilitate the optimisation of therapeutic strategies for SLE and other autoimmune conditions where immune modulation is critical. Furthermore, precise determination of effective dosages can inform future research and clinical practices, leading to innovative therapies that better balance efficacy and safety in the treatment of immune modulation.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIb study was conducted at 12 hospitals (Peking University People’s Hospital, Xinxiang Central Hospital, the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Peking University Shougang Hospital, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University, Peking University Shenzhen Hospital, the First Affiliated Hospital of Wannan Medical College, Peking University Third Hospital, and the First Affiliated Hospital of Baotou Medical College), all located in China from September 2019 to August 2024 (Clinicaltrials.gov registration number: NCT04077684). We aimed to evaluate the dose-dependent efficacy and safety of IL2 (recombinant human IL2 from Escherichia coli) in patients with SLE. Patients with active SLE (SLEDAI-2K ≥ 8), despite receiving standard therapy, were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive IL2 (at a dose of 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 million IU) or placebo for 24 weeks. IL2 or placebo was administered by subcutaneous injection every other day for 12 weeks and then once every week for an additional 12 weeks.

The trial was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The protocol was approved by the institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each site. All participants provided written informed consent. Full details of the trial can be found in the protocol.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Eligible patients were 18–75 years of age and fulfilled the 1997 classification criteria of the American College of Rheumatology for SLE26. Patients had a moderate-to-severe disease activity measured by the SLE Disease Activity Index 2000 (SLEDAI-2K) score of at least 8. Patients had an inadequate response to stable background therapy (dose and type): a SLEDAI-2K score of ≥8 after at least 3 months of continuous treatment with standard-of-care therapies, including prednisone at doses ≤1 mg/kg/day), antimalarial drugs (e.g., hydroxychloroquine), or immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or calcineurin inhibitors) for at least 3 months. The background treatment with corticosteroids, antimalarials, and immunosuppressants was shown in Table 1. Exclusion criteria included: active severe neuropsychiatric manifestations of SLE; history of treatment with rituximab or other biologics; use of high-dose corticosteroids (>1.0 mg/kg) in the preceding month; severe comorbidities including heart failure (≥grade III New York Heart Association), renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance ≤30 mL/min) or hepatic insufficiency (alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase ≥2 times of the upper limit of the normal range); active infection (hepatitis B or C virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV or Mycobacterium tuberculosis); history of chronic infection; malignancy; pregnancy or lactation in females.

sec.title: Randomisation and masking
sec.p: Patients who underwent all screening procedures and met the entry criteria were enroled in the study and assigned to treatment by use of a central interactive wed response system. Patients were randomised in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to placebo, or IL2 at 0.2MIU, 0.5 MIU, or 1 MIU. Patients, investigators and study coordinators were masked to treatment assignment during subcutaneous administration of the drug and assessment of the patients every 4 weeks during the 24-week trial until the database was locked. The interactive web response system was used to assign packages containing double-blind investigational product to each participant. For each patient number and at each patient visit with drug administration, a pharmacist prepared the treatment according to the randomisation list, with labels bearing only the study number of the patient. Placebo was provided as sterile and lyophilised vials were completely matched to those of IL2 for all treatment doses in appearance.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: IL2 at doses of 0.2 MIU, 0.5 MIU, or 1 MIU, or placebo, reconstituted in 1.5 ml of sterile water for injection, was administered subcutaneously every other day for the initial 12 weeks, followed by weekly injections for an additional 12 weeks. A qualified nurse administered the experimental treatment subcutaneously in a day-care ward. Patients were evaluated at screening every 4 weeks until week 24. At each visit, clinical and laboratory parameters were recorded to assess disease activity and safety, and relevant immune cells from peripheral blood were analysed by flow cytometry. Specifically, peripheral blood samples were obtained every four weeks from week 0 to week 24, covering both the induction (IL2 administration every other day for 12 weeks) and maintenance (once a week for 12 weeks). SLE assessment data were collected in real time during a patient’s visit.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who achieved a SRI-4 response at week 12, defined as a reduction by at least 4 points in the SELENA-2K score as compared with baseline, no new British Isles Lupus Assessment Group (BILAG) A or ≤1 new BILAG B score and no deterioration from baseline in the Physician’s Global Assessment (PGA) score by ≥0.3 points27.

Secondary outcomes were the proportion of patients who achieved the Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS), other clinical responses, dynamics of immune cell subsets, and safety, including the change from baseline in SLEDAI-2K score, PGA, and daily dose of GC at week 12 and 24. LLDAS is defined as a SLEDAI-2K ≤ 4, with no activity in major organ systems and no new features of activity compared to previous assessment, and PGA ≤ 1, while receiving a prednisolone (or equivalent) dose of ≤7.5 mg/day and standard maintenance doses of immunosuppressive drugs and approved biological agents28. Absolute changes from baseline in levels of anti-dsDNA and of the complement factors C3 and C4 were analysed at different time points during the study. The numbers and percentages of Tregs and other immune cells were measured by flow cytometry at various time points during the research and the change from baseline was calculated for each patient and treatment arm.

Adverse events (AEs) were recorded from the first dose of study drug through week 24 via scheduled visits, patient diaries, and telephone follow-ups. Only treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) were summarised. Adverse events were coded according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (version 15) and graded according to the WHO Common Toxicity Criteria (version 3.0).

sec.title: Flow cytometry and serological parameters assessment
sec.p: Fresh blood samples were extracted for flow cytometry analysis at each visit. To determine the proportions of T cell subsets in the periphery, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated for cell surface marker staining for flow cytometry analysis. Cells were incubated with APC-CD3, FITC-CD4, PE-CD25, BV510-CD45RA for 30 min, then fixed for 30 min with the eBioscienceTM Foxp3/ Transcription Factor Staining Fixation/Permeabilization Buffer (Invitrogen) and stained for AF647-Foxp3 (Supplementary Table 2). Data was acquired with FACSAria II instrument (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) and analysed with FlowJo software (Tree Star, USA). Regulatory T cells (Tregs) were defined as CD3 + CD4+CD25hiFoxp3+, and Tfh cells were defined as CD3 + CD4 + CXCR5 + PD-1+ (Supplementary Fig. 2). The whole blood was collected and centrifuged to obtain serum. Anti-dsDNA antibody detection with chemiluminescent immunoassay was performed by using the QUANTA Flash dsDNA (Inova Diagnostics, CA, USA), a fully quantitative test operated on the BIO-FLASH instrument (Biokit, Barcelona, Spain). The antigen used was a synthetic antigen coated onto paramagnetic beads. The amount of anti-dsDNA antibodies present in the serum is proportional to the isoluminol conjugate bound to anti-human IgGs. The corresponding relative light units (RLUs) are converted into calculated unitsusing a standard curve. Complement 3 (C3) and complement 4 (C4) levels in serum were determined using a turbidimetric assay (Beckman Coulter DxC 700 AU, Brea, CA, USA). ANA was detected by using indirect immunofluorescence assay on Hep-2 cells (EUROIMMUN Diagnostics).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: We estimated that a sample size of 160 participants would provide at least 85% power to show the superiority of each IL2 dose to placebo with respect to the primary outcome at a two-sided significance level of 0.05. For the sample-size calculations, we assumed at least 35% absolute improvement in the SRI-4 response rate at week 12 between each IL-2 dose group and the placebo group, and a dropout rate of 10%.

For clinical characteristics and laboratory parameters, efficacy outcomes were analysed in the per-protocol (PP) population, excluding patients who discontinued treatment or lacked outcome data and included only patients with complete outcome information. A prespecified mITT analysis, including all randomised patients who initiated treatment and received at least one post-baseline efficacy measurement, was additionally performed to confirm the consistency of results. Differences between the four groups at indicated time points were compared with Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and χ2 test for categorical variables. The safety population comprised all patients who received at least one cycle of study assessment. Safety variables were analysed descriptively with a between-group comparison of the proportions of patients with adverse events. Statistical analysis was performed with the use of SPSS V.27.0. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
